title: Chemical Equilibrium
tagline: Reversible reactions, dynamic equilibrium, the law of mass action, equilibrium constants Kc and Kp, Le Chatelier's principle and the industrial importance of shifting equilibrium — the heart of ISC Class XI physical chemistry.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ISC Class XI Chemistry syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Syllabus unit and chapter title were taken from the official-verified ISC Chemistry registry entry; no board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question. The official CISCE ISC Class XI Chemistry syllabus treats this topic under physical chemistry as the equilibrium chapter, so the content follows that syllabus framing.

overview.intro: Many reactions do not simply run to completion. In a closed vessel, reactants form products, and products can break down again into reactants. Eventually the forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate, and the amounts of reactants and products stop changing. This is chemical equilibrium. The key idea is not that nothing is happening, but that two opposite processes are happening at equal rates. Once students understand that equilibrium is dynamic, the rest of the chapter — the equilibrium constant, its meaning, and the effect of changing conditions — becomes much easier to see as a coherent whole rather than as a list of separate rules.

facts.label: Core ideas
facts.value: Reversible reactions; dynamic equilibrium; law of mass action; equilibrium constant Kc and Kp; relationship between Kc and Kp; Le Chatelier's principle; effect of concentration, temperature, pressure and catalyst; industrial applications

learningOutcomes: Explain what is meant by a reversible reaction and by chemical equilibrium.
State that equilibrium is dynamic and describe what that means.
State the law of mass action and write the expression for the equilibrium constant Kc for a given reaction.
Compare Kc and Kp and relate them where appropriate.
Interpret the magnitude of the equilibrium constant in terms of the position of equilibrium.
State Le Chatelier's principle and predict the effect of changes in concentration, pressure, temperature and the presence of a catalyst.
Explain the importance of equilibrium principles in some industrial processes.
Distinguish between the effect of a catalyst and the effect of other changes on equilibrium.

blocks.text: A reversible reaction is one that can go in both directions under the same conditions. Reactants give products, and products can give reactants again. In a closed system, such a reaction does not just stop when the reactants are used up. Instead, as products build up, the reverse reaction becomes faster, and eventually the forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate. At that point the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant, even though both reactions are still taking place. This state is called dynamic equilibrium.

items: A reversible reaction can proceed in both the forward and reverse directions.
In dynamic equilibrium, the forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate.
The concentrations of reactants and products remain constant at equilibrium.
Equilibrium can be reached only in a closed system.
Dynamic equilibrium does not mean the reaction has stopped.

items.text: Consider a reaction in a closed vessel. At first only reactants are present, so the forward reaction is fastest. As products form, the reverse reaction increases. Eventually the two rates become equal. The mixture looks unchanged from the outside, but inside it is active in both directions.
items.note: This picture is more useful than the misleading idea that equilibrium means 'everything is finished'.

learn.title: The law of mass action and the equilibrium constant

blocks.text: The law of mass action relates the concentrations of reactants and products at equilibrium to a constant for the reaction at a given temperature. For a general reversible reaction, the equilibrium constant expression is written as the product of the concentrations of the products divided by the product of the concentrations of the reactants, each raised to the power of its stoichiometric coefficient. The value of this constant depends only on temperature for a given reaction, not on the starting amounts.

items: The equilibrium constant Kc is defined using molar concentrations.
Each concentration is raised to the power of its coefficient in the balanced equation.
Kc depends on temperature, not on initial concentrations.
The expression does not include pure solids or pure liquids.
The form of the expression depends on the way the equation is written.

items.text: For a reaction aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, the equilibrium constant Kc = [C]^c [D]^d / [A]^a [B]^b, where the square brackets denote equilibrium concentrations. If the reaction is written in reverse, the equilibrium constant becomes the reciprocal of the original value, which is why the equation must always be stated clearly.
items.note: The example shows why the balanced equation matters every time the constant is written.

blocks.text: A useful way to think about Kc is as a number that tells how far a reaction proceeds before equilibrium is established at a given temperature. A large Kc means the equilibrium mixture contains mostly products; a small Kc means it contains mostly reactants. This is a qualitative guide, not a complete description, but it helps students interpret the constant rather than just calculate it.

learn.title: Kp and the relation between Kc and Kp

blocks.text: For reactions involving gases, it is often convenient to use partial pressures instead of concentrations. The equilibrium constant in terms of partial pressures is written as Kp. For the same reaction, Kp and Kc are related, but they are not identical unless the number of moles of gaseous reactants and gaseous products is the same. The relationship depends on the change in the number of moles of gas, the gas constant and the temperature. Students should remember that both Kc and Kp describe the same equilibrium at the same temperature; they are just different ways of expressing it.

items: Kp is the equilibrium constant expressed in terms of partial pressures.
Kc and Kp are related through the change in moles of gas.
If there is no change in the number of moles of gas, Kc and Kp may be numerically equal.
Both constants are temperature dependent.

items.text: If a reaction has the same number of moles of gas on both sides, a change in pressure does not alter the position of equilibrium, though it may affect the rate at which equilibrium is reached. If the number of moles differs, pressure can shift the equilibrium, and this is where Le Chatelier's principle becomes practically important.
items.note: This sets up the later discussion of pressure effects without confusing rate and equilibrium position.

blocks.text: Le Chatelier's principle is a general rule for predicting how an equilibrium system responds to a change. It states that if a change is imposed on a system at equilibrium, the system shifts in a direction that tends to counteract the change. The principle does not explain why the shift happens in mechanistic detail, but it is a reliable guide for concentration, pressure and temperature changes. It is important to apply it carefully, one change at a time, and not to treat every change as if it affected the equilibrium constant.

items: Increasing the concentration of a reactant shifts the equilibrium toward more products.
Increasing the concentration of a product shifts the equilibrium toward more reactants.
Changing pressure affects equilibrium only if there is a change in the number of moles of gas.
Temperature changes alter the equilibrium constant for reactions with a heat term.
A catalyst does not shift the position of equilibrium; it helps the system reach equilibrium faster.

items.text: In an exothermic reaction, heat can be thought of as a product. Raising the temperature therefore shifts the equilibrium in the endothermic direction, which is the reverse direction for an exothermic reaction. In an endothermic reaction, the opposite happens. Students often remember the rule more easily when they connect temperature to the heat term in the equation.
items.note: Linking temperature to the exothermic/endothermic character of the reaction helps prevent a memorized but empty statement of the principle.

learn.title: Effects of changes and common misconceptions

blocks.text: One of the most important distinctions in this chapter is between the effect of a change on the position of equilibrium and the effect on the equilibrium constant. Only temperature changes the equilibrium constant itself. Concentration and pressure changes can shift the position of equilibrium, but they do not change Kc or Kp at constant temperature. A catalyst speeds up both forward and reverse reactions equally, so it does not change the position of equilibrium; it only shortens the time needed to reach equilibrium. These distinctions are frequent sources of mistakes in examination answers.

items: Concentration changes shift the position of equilibrium but not the equilibrium constant.
Pressure changes shift equilibrium only when the gas moles differ on the two sides.
Temperature changes the equilibrium constant.
A catalyst does not change the equilibrium position.
At equilibrium, the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal.

items.text: If more reactant is added to a system at equilibrium, the system responds by making more product, but Kc stays the same at that temperature. If a student says that Kc increases because more product now forms, the mistake is to confuse a change in position with a change in the constant itself.
items.note: This example targets a very common error and separates the two ideas explicitly.

blocks.text: Equilibrium principles are not just theoretical. In industry, reactions are often run under conditions chosen to give a good yield and a good rate at the same time. Since rate and equilibrium are different matters, engineers and chemists have to balance them. A catalyst may be used to reach equilibrium quickly, while temperature and pressure are chosen with the equilibrium position in mind. The industrial importance of equilibrium is a good reason to learn the chapter carefully: the same principles appear again and again in real processes.

items: Industrial processes use equilibrium ideas to improve yield and efficiency.
Rate and equilibrium position are separate considerations.
Temperature and pressure are chosen with both chemistry and economics in mind.
Catalysts help attain equilibrium faster without changing its position.

items.text: In a reversible manufacturing process, a high pressure may favor the product side if the product side has fewer gas moles, but too high a pressure may be costly. A moderate temperature may give a better balance between yield and speed. These are practical versions of the same principles studied in the chapter.
items.note: The example connects the textbook chapter to real decision-making without inventing a syllabus requirement.

keyPoints: Chemical equilibrium is dynamic; forward and reverse reactions occur at equal rates.
The equilibrium constant Kc is defined from the balanced equation and equilibrium concentrations.
Kc depends on temperature, not on initial concentrations.
Kp is used for gaseous equilibria and is related to Kc through the change in gas moles.
Le Chatelier's principle predicts how equilibrium shifts in response to changes.
Only temperature changes the equilibrium constant; concentration and pressure change the position.
A catalyst speeds up reaching equilibrium but does not shift its position.
Rate and equilibrium position are different and must not be confused.
examFocus: Always write the equilibrium constant expression from the balanced equation as given.
Remember to exclude pure solids and pure liquids from the Kc expression.
Do not claim that a catalyst changes the equilibrium position.
State clearly whether a change affects position, rate, or the equilibrium constant.
Use Le Chatelier's principle carefully and consistently with the reaction's exothermic or endothermic character.

vocabulary.meaning: A reaction that can proceed in both forward and reverse directions under the same conditions.
A state in which the forward and reverse reactions occur at equal rates so concentrations remain constant.
A number that expresses the ratio of product and reactant concentrations or pressures at equilibrium at a given temperature.
The equilibrium constant expressed in terms of molar concentrations.
The equilibrium constant expressed in terms of partial pressures.
The principle that a system at equilibrium shifts to counteract an imposed change.
The relative amounts of reactants and products present at equilibrium.

questions.prompt: At chemical equilibrium, the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are:
questions.explanation: At equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking equilibrium means all reaction has stopped.

questions.prompt: A reversible reaction attains equilibrium only in a:
questions.explanation: Equilibrium requires that reactants and products remain in the system so the reverse reaction can occur.
questions.commonMistake: Forgetting that escape of products prevents equilibrium in an open system.

questions.prompt: The equilibrium constant Kc for a reaction depends mostly on:
questions.explanation: Kc is constant at a given temperature and changes only when temperature changes.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking that concentration or volume changes Kc.

questions.prompt: For a reaction aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, the correct Kc expression is:
questions.explanation: Kc is the product concentrations raised to their coefficients divided by the reactant concentrations raised to theirs.
questions.commonMistake: Flipping numerator and denominator or forgetting the stoichiometric powers.

questions.prompt: In the equilibrium constant expression, pure solids and pure liquids are:
questions.explanation: Pure solids and pure liquids do not appear in the equilibrium constant expression.
questions.commonMistake: Putting solids or liquids into the expression like gases or solutions.

questions.prompt: If Kc is very large for a reaction at a given temperature, the equilibrium mixture contains mainly:
options: Equal amounts of reactants and products
questions.explanation: A large Kc means the equilibrium lies far to the product side.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing a large constant with equal or reactant-dominated mixtures.

questions.prompt: Which change will alter the value of the equilibrium constant at constant temperature?
questions.explanation: At constant temperature, Kc does not change due to concentration, pressure or a catalyst.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking that adding reactant or a catalyst changes Kc.

questions.prompt: For a gaseous equilibrium where the number of moles of gas is greater on the reactant side, increasing pressure at constant temperature will:
options: Have no effect on the position
questions.explanation: Increasing pressure favors the side with fewer moles of gas, which is the product side here, so the reverse is true when reactants have more moles.
questions.commonMistake: Remembering the pressure rule but applying it backwards.

questions.prompt: In an exothermic reversible reaction, raising the temperature shifts equilibrium:
options: Only if a catalyst is present
questions.explanation: For an exothermic reaction, adding heat favors the reverse, endothermic direction.
questions.commonMistake: Applying the temperature rule without considering whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.

questions.answer: If a change is imposed on a system at equilibrium, the system shifts in a direction that tends to counteract the change.
questions.explanation: The principle predicts the direction of shift when concentration, pressure or temperature is changed.
questions.commonMistake: Stating the principle too vaguely, without mentioning the tendency to counteract the change.

questions.prompt: Explain why a catalyst does not change the position of equilibrium.
questions.answer: A catalyst speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster but the relative amounts of reactants and products remain the same.
questions.explanation: The catalyst changes rate, not the equilibrium position.
questions.commonMistake: Saying that a catalyst increases the yield of product.

questions.prompt: Why is the equilibrium described as dynamic?
questions.answer: Because at equilibrium both the forward and reverse reactions continue to occur, but at equal rates, so the overall concentrations stay constant.
questions.explanation: Dynamic means active, not static; reactions continue at equal rates.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking dynamic equilibrium means the reaction has stopped.

questions.prompt: If the equilibrium constant for a reaction written in one direction is K, the equilibrium constant for the reverse reaction is:
questions.explanation: The reverse reaction has the reciprocal equilibrium constant.
questions.commonMistake: Forgetting that reversing the equation inverts the constant.

questions.prompt: A reaction involving only gases has the same number of moles on both sides. Which statement is correct?
options: Pressure changes will shift the equilibrium position.
Pressure changes will not shift the equilibrium position.
questions.answer: Pressure changes will not shift the equilibrium position.
questions.explanation: When gas moles are equal, pressure does not favor either side.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming pressure always shifts equilibrium, regardless of mole change.

questions.prompt: Why does the equilibrium constant have different values at different temperatures?
questions.answer: Because the equilibrium constant depends on temperature; changing temperature changes the relative rates of the forward and reverse reactions and therefore the equilibrium position and constant.
questions.explanation: Temperature is the key factor that changes the value of the equilibrium constant.
questions.commonMistake: Attributing changes in Kc to concentration or pressure instead of temperature.
